shots.title: Scan everything
shots.engineer: A rider opens the app and asks: which drivers are within a kilometre of me? Or a shopper asks for the nearest open shop. The simplest answer is to work out the distance from the rider to every driver in the table, sort, and keep the closest. That is fine for a hundred rows. With every driver in every city, it means reading the whole table and doing the maths for each row, on every request, many times a second.
shots.executive: Answering "what is near me" by measuring the distance to everything works for a small list, but becomes far too slow once there are millions of places.

shots.title: Index latitude
shots.engineer: The obvious fix is an ordinary index on latitude, and maybe another on longitude, then a bounding box: latitude between a and b, longitude between c and d. But a B-tree sorts by one column at a time. The latitude index returns a thin strip that runs right round the planet, every driver in that band, from London to Calgary. The database then throws most of them away on longitude. Two separate indexes do not combine into a two-dimensional one.
shots.executive: Indexing latitude and longitude separately still pulls in a whole band around the world and throws most of it away.

shots.title: Cells
shots.engineer: The pattern is to turn two dimensions into one. Divide the surface into cells, give each cell an id, and store every object under the id of the cell it sits in. Now an ordinary index works again. To search, find the cell containing the query point, add its neighbouring cells so the radius is covered, and look up just those few keys. That returns candidates, not answers, so a final exact distance check drops anything outside the radius and sorts the rest.
shots.executive: Divide the map into numbered cells and file everything by cell. To search, look in your cell and the ones around it, then measure only those.

shots.title: Geohash, trees, S2, H3
shots.engineer: There are four common ways to cut the globe. Geohash interleaves latitude and longitude bits into a base-32 string; a longer shared prefix means closer. Trees, such as the R-tree PostGIS builds on GiST, nest bounding boxes. Google's S2 projects the Earth onto a cube and numbers cells along a Hilbert curve, with sixty-four-bit ids and levels from nought to thirty. Uber's H3 uses hexagons on an icosahedron, with sixteen resolutions, each with about a seventh of the area of the one above.
shots.executive: Geohash, tree indexes, Google's S2 and Uber's H3 are four ways to cut up the map. They differ in cell shape and how neighbours are found.

shots.title: Nearby query
shots.engineer: Step by step with H3. The rider asks for drivers within one kilometre. The service asks the library for the rider's cell at resolution eight, where an average hexagon is about seven tenths of a square kilometre. Then it asks for a grid disk of radius one: that cell plus its six neighbours. It looks up who is in those seven cells, gets a list of candidates, computes the true distance to each, drops anything beyond a kilometre, sorts, and returns the nearest.
shots.executive: The service finds your hexagon and the six around it, collects everyone in them, then measures the real distance to each and returns the closest.

shots.title: Moving objects
shots.engineer: Shops do not move, but drivers do. If each one reports its position every few seconds, the index takes far more writes than reads, so it is usually kept in memory, keyed by cell. Each update computes the cell id. If the driver is still in the same cell, only the point changes. If they have crossed into a new cell, remove them from the old one and add them to the new. Drivers who stop reporting expire, so the map never shows ghosts.
shots.executive: For things that move, keep the cell map in memory, move each driver between cells as they report in, and drop anyone who goes quiet.

shots.title: Cell edges
shots.engineer: The first trap is the cell edge. A shared geohash prefix means two points are close, but the reverse is not true. Stand near the edge of your cell and the nearest shop may sit fifty metres away in the next cell, with a completely different prefix. Points either side of the Equator, the Greenwich meridian or the hundred-and-eightieth meridian can share no prefix at all. A prefix-only search misses them. The fix is always the same: search the neighbouring cells too.
shots.executive: Something just across a cell border can be very close yet look far away by its code. Always search the neighbouring cells as well.

shots.title: Hot and empty cells
shots.engineer: The second trap is density. People are not spread evenly. A city centre at rush hour can put thousands of drivers in one cell, so every query there drags back a long candidate list, and if you shard by cell, one shard takes the load. Use finer cells where it is dense, or split a hot cell's key further. The countryside has the opposite problem: ring one is empty. Grow the ring step by step until you have enough results or reach a sensible limit.
shots.executive: Busy city cells hold too much and quiet rural cells hold nothing. Use smaller cells where it is crowded and search further out where it is empty.

card.heading: Which grid?
points: Geohash | A string; prefix ranges in any index · uneven cells, seams at edges
R-tree (PostGIS GiST) | Any shape, exact queries in SQL · tree updates on every move
S2 | Square cells, 4 children each, levels 0–30, region coverings · neighbours at two distances
H3 | Equal-distance neighbours, rings · children only roughly fit parents; 12 pentagons

shots.engineer: Comparing them. Geohash is just a string, so any database can index it, but cells change shape with latitude and the seams cause the edge problem. An R-tree, like PostGIS GiST, handles any shape with exact SQL queries, at the cost of tree updates on every write. S2 gives square cells that split cleanly into four children, and good region coverings. H3's hexagons have every neighbour at the same distance, which makes rings natural, but children only roughly fit their parents, and there are twelve pentagons.
shots.executive: Geohash is simplest, tree indexes suit databases and shapes, S2 suits covering regions, and H3 suits rings of equal neighbours.

card.heading: Choosing a resolution
points: Cell about the size of a typical search radius
Too coarse: long candidate lists to filter
Too fine: many cells to look up per query
Dense areas may need finer cells than rural ones
Skip the index when the data fits in memory and a scan is fast enough

shots.engineer: Choosing a resolution is the main tuning decision. A good starting point is a cell about the size of your typical search radius, so one ring covers it. Too coarse, and every query returns a long list to filter. Too fine, and each query must look up many cells. Dense areas may want finer cells than rural ones. And when not to bother: if you have a few thousand points that fit in memory, a plain scan is simple and fast enough.
shots.executive: Pick cells about the size of a typical search. Too big wastes filtering, too small wastes lookups, and small datasets may not need an index at all.

shots.title: Implementations
shots.engineer: In the wild. Uber open-sourced H3 in twenty eighteen and uses it for pricing and dispatch; the core is a C library under Apache two. Google's S2 Geometry library is Apache licensed too. PostGIS builds an R-tree on GiST, filters by bounding box, then runs the exact test. Redis stores a fifty-two-bit geohash as a sorted-set score and checks nine areas per search. Elasticsearch has geo point fields and geohash grid aggregations, and MongoDB's two-d-sphere index returns results nearest first.
shots.executive: Uber's H3 and Google's S2 are open-source cell libraries. PostGIS, Redis, Elasticsearch and MongoDB all build spatial indexes into the database.

card.heading: Neighbours
points: Sharding | Cell id makes a natural shard key; watch hot cities
Consistent hashing | Spreads cells over nodes so few move when you add one
Event streaming | Carries the flood of position updates into the index
Caching | Popular cells' results reused for a few seconds

shots.engineer: Its neighbours. Sharding: a coarse cell id makes a natural shard key, keeping a neighbourhood on one machine, but dense cities become hot shards. Consistent hashing spreads cells across nodes so that adding a node moves only a few. Event streaming carries the flood of position updates from phones into the in-memory index. And a short cache in front of popular cells lets many riders in the same area share one lookup for a few seconds.
shots.executive: A geospatial index often sits on sharding, uses consistent hashing to spread cells, and is fed by a stream of location updates.

card.heading: Recap
points: Turn 2-D location into 1-D cell ids, then use an ordinary index
Query your cell plus its neighbours, then filter by exact distance
Pick a resolution to match your radius and density

shots.engineer: Three things to remember. Turn two-dimensional location into one-dimensional cell ids, with geohash, S2, H3 or a spatial tree, so an ordinary index can do the work. Always query your own cell plus its neighbours, because the nearest thing may be just across a border, and finish with an exact distance check. And choose the resolution to match your search radius and your density, adapting where cities crowd and the countryside empties.
shots.executive: File places by map cell. Search your cell and its neighbours, then measure. Size the cells to fit the search.

meta.blurb: File locations by map cell so "what is near me" looks up a few cells instead of scanning the world.
